scenes.heading: Vaccines and immunotherapy
scenes.say: Vaccines are one of the most effective tools medicine has ever had. Scientists can now also make antibodies in the lab and use them as drugs. Let's see how both work.

scenes.heading: Four types of immunity
points: Natural passive: placenta or breast milk
scenes.say: Ask two questions. Did my own immune system make the antibodies? If yes, it's active, and long-lasting. If no, it's passive: immediate but short-lived. Was there a medical intervention? Yes means artificial, no means natural. So a vaccine is artificial active, and antivenom is artificial passive.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A practice match against the opposition's reserves
scenes.science: A vaccine shows your immune system the antigens without the disease
scenes.breaks: teams learn by thinking, but immune memory comes from clonal selection and expansion of matching lymphocytes.
scenes.say: A vaccine is like a practice match against the other team's reserves. Same jerseys, same plays, but no star players. Your immune system goes through the slow primary response safely, and keeps memory cells. If the real pathogen turns up, it meets a fast, strong secondary response. A booster is an extra practice session.

scenes.heading: Types of vaccine
points: mRNA and viral vector: cells make antigen
scenes.say: Live attenuated vaccines use a weakened pathogen. Inactivated vaccines use a killed one. Subunit vaccines use selected antigens, and toxoids use an inactivated toxin. With m R N A and viral vector vaccines, your own cells briefly make the antigen. The m R N A never changes your DNA.
scenes.caption: Live attenuated vaccines use a weakened pathogen. Inactivated vaccines use a killed one. Subunit vaccines use selected antigens, and toxoids use an inactivated toxin. With mRNA and viral vector vaccines, your own cells briefly make the antigen. The mRNA never changes your DNA.

scenes.heading: Herd immunity
scenes.question: Town A is mostly vaccinated; Town B only about half. One infected traveller visits each. What happens?
lines: Town A: traveller meets mostly immune people
Town B: many susceptible people infected
scenes.say: In Town A, the traveller mostly meets immune people, so transmission chains end. In Town B, many people are susceptible, so the disease spreads. Herd immunity protects people who can't be vaccinated, like newborns. The more contagious the disease, the more people need to be immune.

scenes.heading: Making monoclonal antibodies
steps: Inject a mouse with the antigen
Select and clone the right hybridoma
scenes.say: Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies from one clone of cells. A plasma cell knows how to make the antibody but can't divide in culture. A myeloma cell divides forever. Fuse them into a hybridoma, and it makes one antibody, endlessly.

scenes.heading: Immunotherapy with mAbs

right.title: Autoimmunity: turn down
points: Remove or block harmful immune cells

scenes.say: For cancer, monoclonal antibodies turn the immune response up: marking cancer cells, blocking growth signals, or releasing the brakes on T cells. For autoimmune disease, they turn it down, for example by neutralising TNF. It's passive, so doses must be repeated.

points: Active vs passive; natural vs artificial
scenes.say: Quick recap. Vaccines give artificial active immunity with memory cells. Herd immunity protects the vulnerable. Hybridomas make monoclonal antibodies, used to turn the immune response up or down. Now try the practice questions!
